The `week` of a competency is the General English programme week it teaches (weeks.json), NOT the order these were built: Week 1 'Explain what you do' — 5 moves; Week 2 'Give a clear update' — 4 moves; Week 3 'Raise a problem' — 5 moves; Week 4 'Clarifying, asking questions & confirming' — 4 moves (flag → ask → restate → confirm), no shadow block after a content check (see its _shadow_note); Week 5 'Explaining technical work to non-technical stakeholders' — 4 moves (frame → plain → impact → check), no shadow block after a content check (see its _shadow_note); Week 6 'Recommendations & decision language' — 5 moves (options → recommend → reason → tradeoff → next), no shadow block after a content check (see its _shadow_note); Week 7 'Disagreeing professionally & pushing back' — 5 moves (acknowledge → disagree → reason → alternative → align), shadow block linked to mmfo9spNaWA (925 English Lesson 11, 'How to Disagree and Say No in English') after a content check — it models the first three moves and its shadow.why says so (see also its _shadow_note). The first two were prototyped as 2 and 3 and were renumbered once the third arrived; `week` is display, analytics and the pickNext tie-break only — every store, route and record is keyed by competency id, so nothing had to be migrated. OPTIONAL curriculum section, General English only. A track without its own missions.json gets null, NOT the parent's: professional-tracks.js lists 'missions' in NEVER_INHERIT precisely so this content can never reach Welding through the curriculum merge. Content is written in English like every other pack (weeks.json, phrases.json); only the surrounding chrome is translated through t().

competencies.title: Explain what you do
competencies.objective: Explain your role and your current work so that someone who has never met your team understands it.
competencies.pattern: ROLE → RESPONSIBILITY → RIGHT NOW → WHO IT'S FOR → WHY IT MATTERS
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block on purpose. The 301-clip General English library has nothing about describing your own role — the nearest match is about expressing opinions — and inventing a link would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. The NOTICE step simply omits the Shadow row, and fromShadow() never links a clip to a competency that names none. Add a "shadow" block here the day a fitting clip exists.

moves.label: Role
moves.hint: What you are and where you sit. Name it in one short sentence.
patterns: I work as a logistics analyst.
My role sits between operations and finance.
I'm the person who looks after the supplier data.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by naming your job and the team you sit in.

moves.label: Responsibility
moves.hint: What is actually yours — the part that would go wrong without you.
patterns: I'm responsible for the weekly reports.
A big part of my role is checking supplier data.
I look after everything that leaves the warehouse.
moves.retry: Say it again and name one thing you are responsible for — the part that is yours.
cues: a big part of my role

moves.label: Right now
moves.hint: What is on your desk this week, not what you did last year.
patterns: At the moment I'm rebuilding the tracking sheet.
This week I'm focused on the supplier audit.
Right now we're moving everything onto the new system.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what you are working on at the moment.

moves.label: Who it's for
moves.hint: Who you work with, or who receives what you produce.
patterns: I work closely with the warehouse managers.
It goes to the finance team every Monday.
My main users are the people on the shop floor.
moves.retry: Say it again and say who you work with, or who your work is for.

moves.label: Why it matters
moves.hint: What it is for. The result, not the task.
patterns: …so the team can see a problem before the customer does.
It means nothing leaves the site unchecked.
The point is that nobody has to chase it by hand.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with what your work is actually for — what it makes possible.

expressions.def: the plain way to open with your job title

expressions.w: my role sits at the intersection of
expressions.def: for a job that spans two teams
names what you own

expressions.w: a big part of my role is
expressions.def: introduces your main responsibility
what is on your desk at the moment
names the people you depend on
learn what you need to know about something new
in agreement, sharing the same understanding

see.where: It is your first week. You are at lunch with someone from another department.
see.asks: So what do you actually do here?
see.goal: Answer in about 30 seconds so that someone outside your team understands your job and why it exists.

hear.model: I work as an operations analyst in the logistics team. I'm responsible for the weekly delivery reports and the supplier data. At the moment I'm rebuilding how we track late shipments. I work closely with the warehouse managers, so the team can see a problem before it reaches the customer.
hear.note: Five short sentences. One move each. No job title jargon.

missions.prompt: So what do you actually do here?
missions.context: They do not know your team, your tools or your acronyms. Assume they know nothing about your work except that it happens in this building.

see.where: A video call is starting with a client who has never met your team.
see.asks: Before we start — can you tell us a bit about your role?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time, and this is a first impression with someone outside the company.

missions.prompt: Before we start — can you tell us a bit about your role?
missions.context: They are paying for the work. They want to know who they are talking to and why you are the right person to be on this call.

competencies.title: Give a clear update
competencies.objective: Give a concise professional project update that a busy colleague can act on.

shadow.title: How to Organize Your Thoughts When Speaking English (Stop Rambling)
shadow.why: The same four-part shape, spoken at natural pace by a professional speaker.

moves.label: Status
moves.hint: Where the work actually is right now.
patterns: The project is on track.
We've completed the first two stages.
So far, everything is going to plan.
moves.retry: Give the update again and open with one clear sentence saying where the work is right now.
moves._cue_note: Phrase cues, not bare words. A single cue like "ready" or "done" would fire inside a next-step sentence ("we'll be ready tomorrow") and credit a status the learner never gave. Under-crediting is the safe direction here: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed, and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner only a retry.

moves.label: Issue
moves.hint: The one thing that is not going to plan.
patterns: We've run into a supplier issue.
We're held up waiting for approval.
The problem is a delay at the supplier.
moves.retry: Give the update again and name the one problem clearly, in a single sentence.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it means for the deadline, the cost or the customer. This is the move most people skip.
patterns: This may affect Friday's delivery.
It puts the deadline at risk.
That means we'd be two days late.
moves.retry: Give the update again and say clearly what the delay means for the deadline — name the date or the number of days.

moves.label: Next step
moves.hint: What you are doing about it, and when you will report back.
patterns: We're working with the supplier.
I'll have an update for you tomorrow.
The next step is to confirm a new date.
moves.retry: Give the update again and finish by saying what you will do next and when you will report back.

expressions.def: going to plan, at the expected point
delayed by something outside your control
meet an unexpected problem
the further result a delay causes elsewhere
likely to fail or be missed
move a date later
contact someone to make something happen
report again later with an answer

see.where: You are in a project meeting.
see.asks: Can you give us a quick update on the project?
see.goal: Answer in about 30 seconds so that everyone in the room knows where things stand and what happens next.

hear.model: The project is progressing well. We're currently delayed by a supplier issue. This may affect Friday's delivery. We're working with the supplier and expect an update tomorrow.
hear.note: Four short sentences. One move each. No preamble.

missions.prompt: Can you give us a quick update on the project?
missions.context: Your team is building a new customer portal. Two of the three stages are finished. The design agency has not sent the final logo files, and the launch is planned for Friday.

see.where: You are at your desk. The warehouse has just called.
see.asks: The supplier delivered the materials late. What does this mean for the project?
see.goal: Nobody is going to prompt you this time. Use the same four moves on a situation you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: The supplier delivered the materials late. What does this mean for the project?
missions.context: The materials arrived three days late. Installation was due to start on Monday. The customer has been promised the site by the end of the month.

competencies.title: Raise a problem
competencies.objective: Explain a problem, what caused it and what it costs, then ask for the decision or the help you actually need.
competencies.pattern: ISSUE → CAUSE → IMPACT → WHAT I'VE DONE → WHAT I NEED

shadow.title: Business English - 925 English Lesson 33 - How to Explain a Problem in English
shadow.why: A lesson on this exact job: state the problem generally, tell the story of what caused it, and ask for help politely. It models three of the five moves — issue, cause and ask — and not impact or what you have already done, so it supports this competency without standing in for it.

moves.label: The problem
moves.hint: Name it in one sentence, before any of the story. A listener who does not know what is wrong cannot follow what happened.
patterns: We've got a problem with the delivery.
There's an issue with the monthly figures.
The machine on line two has stopped.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with one short sentence naming what is wrong — before you explain how it happened.

moves.label: Cause
moves.hint: What actually happened, in the past tense. Be specific about the event, not about whose fault it was.
patterns: It started when the supplier changed our order number.
What happened was the report got switched off in August.
The delay was caused by a late delivery.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what actually happened — one sentence in the past tense, naming the event that started it.
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "because". "I'm raising it because it affects Friday" is an impact sentence, and crediting it as a cause would tell a learner they had explained what happened when they had not.

moves.label: Impact
moves.hint: What it costs: the date, the money or the customer. Without this nobody knows how hard to work on it.
patterns: This means installation cannot start on Monday.
We would finish three days late.
It puts the Thursday board pack at risk.
moves.retry: Say it again and say what the problem costs — name the date, the days or the person who feels it.

moves.label: What I've done
moves.hint: The step you have already taken. It is what stops a problem sounding like a complaint.
patterns: I've already spoken to their office.
In the meantime we're using the old report.
We've put a temporary fix in place.
moves.retry: Say it again and add the one thing you have already done about it, before you say what you need.
moves._cue_note: Narrow on purpose, and narrower than it looks. A bare "we've already" fires inside "we've already lost two days", which is an impact statement — it would credit the learner with handling a problem they had only described. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one, so a strict floor costs an online learner nothing and an offline learner one retry.

moves.label: What I need
moves.hint: The decision, the person or the permission you want. This is the move almost everyone leaves out, and it is the reason for speaking at all.
patterns: Could you approve the courier cost?
Would you mind chasing them at your level?
What I need from you is a decision on the date.
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with a plain question — what do you need this person to decide, approve or do?
cues: what would you like me to

expressions.def: raise something early, before it becomes a surprise
the thing that actually started it, not what you noticed first
cost us time we had already planned to use
fail to finish by the agreed date
a temporary way round a problem while it is being fixed
in the time before it is properly fixed
formally approve something so the work can go ahead
a polite way to ask someone to do something

see.where: You are at your desk. The work has stopped, and your manager is walking past.
see.asks: You look worried — what's going on?
see.goal: Explain it in about 30 seconds, so your manager knows what is wrong, what it costs, and what you need from them.

hear.model: We've got a problem with the delivery. It started when the supplier changed our order number. This means installation cannot start on Monday, so we would finish three days late. I've already spoken to their office and asked them for a new date. Could you approve the courier cost if they can get the parts here on Saturday?
hear.note: Five short sentences. One move each. The ask comes last, and it is a real question.

missions.prompt: You look worried — what's going on?
missions.context: The parts for Monday's installation have not arrived. The supplier changed the order number and the shipment went to the wrong depot. The customer has been promised the site by the end of the month. A Saturday courier would cost extra.

see.where: You are in Monday's team meeting. The problem is not yours — you are just the one who found it.
see.who: The project lead, in front of the team
see.asks: Anything anyone wants to raise before we finish?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time, and the whole team is listening. Use the same five moves on a problem you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: Anything anyone wants to raise before we finish?
missions.context: On Friday you noticed the monthly figures are coming from a report that was switched off in August. Two months of numbers may be wrong. The board pack goes out on Thursday.

competencies.title: Clarifying, asking questions & confirming
competencies.objective: Stop staying silent when something is unclear: say that it is, ask one precise question, say back what you heard, and confirm what happens next.
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The audit's candidate 54ebEjg4EM8 ('Ask Better Questions') is about deepening personal conversation and contains none of this competency's language. The nearest real content is kBlTRXvZlCE ('How to Be Taken Seriously as a New Manager'), which models asking a precise question and 'here's what I'm hearing so far' as leadership signalling, and v60wdYHP4kA ('Building Trust'), which teaches 'let me make sure I understood you — you said…' as active listening. Neither is about clarifying an unclear instruction at work and neither models confirming the next step, so linking one would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. Revisit when the library has a clip on this exact job; a reviewer may choose to link kBlTRXvZlCE.

moves.label: Flag the gap
moves.hint: Say plainly that something is not clear to you yet. One sentence, before any question — a listener who does not know you are lost cannot help you.
patterns: Sorry, one thing isn't clear to me yet.
I'm not sure I follow the timeline.
Just to make sure I understand this properly…
moves.retry: Say it again and open by saying plainly that something is not clear yet — before you ask your question.
cues: make sure i get this right
make sure we're on the same page
make sure we are on the same page
one thing i am not sure
one thing i want to check
one thing i need to check
one thing i'd like to check
one thing i would like to check
i would like to be sure
moves._cue_note: Openers only: the move is admitting the gap, not asking about it. "Just to confirm" and "so to confirm" are deliberately absent everywhere in this competency — spoken before a paraphrase they are a flag, spoken before a plan they are a confirmation, and crediting either move from them would guess.

moves.label: Ask one question
moves.hint: One precise question about the thing you are missing — the date, the person, the scope or the number. "Can you explain?" is not precise.
patterns: When you say soon, do you mean before Friday's review?
Are you asking for the full report or just the summary?
What timeline are we working against?
moves.retry: Say it again and ask one precise question — name the exact thing you need to know: the date, the person, the number or the scope.
cues: could you give me an example
can you give me an example
what does it need to include
moves._cue_note: Deliberately no bare "do you want" or "would you like". "Do you want me to start today?" is a question about the next step, not about the gap — it belongs to confirm if anywhere, and crediting the ask from it would tell a learner they had pinned down the instruction when they had not. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move the cues missed and can never remove one.

moves.label: Say it back
moves.hint: Repeat the instruction in your own words — what, by when, for whom. It is how the other person hears the gap before it turns into a mistake.
patterns: So you're saying you need the March metrics on the new dashboard, before Friday.
If I've understood correctly, the client wants the quote today and the date can follow.
So the priority is the summary — the full report can wait.
moves.retry: Say it again and say back what you heard, in your own words — what, by when and for whom — before you commit to anything.
cues: if i have got that right
if i have got this right
correct me if i am wrong
moves._cue_note: No bare "is that right" or "is that correct": tagged onto a plan ("I'll send it Friday, is that right?") they close a confirmation, and crediting a paraphrase from them would guess. "Did I get that right?" stays, because it can only follow something said back.

moves.label: Confirm the next step
moves.hint: Close with what happens now — who does what, by when — and get a yes. Without this, nothing was actually agreed.
patterns: So to summarise what we agreed: I'll send the summary by Thursday.
Then I'll start on the March numbers today and check in with you tomorrow — does that work?
Before we move on, can we confirm the review is Wednesday afternoon?
moves.retry: Say it again and finish by confirming the next step — who does what, by when — and ask for a yes.
cues: i will come back to you
i will get back to you
moves._cue_note: A confirmation is a commitment ("then I'll…") or an explicit agreement check ("can we confirm…", "does that work?"). A deadline on its own ("by Friday") is not one — it belongs just as naturally inside a paraphrase — so no day or date is a cue here.

expressions.w: just to make sure I understand
expressions.def: a polite way to say you are about to check something before you act
a short, polite way to say you have lost the thread
ask someone to say exactly what a word or phrase covers
explain something step by step, from the start
the words that begin a paraphrase of what you just heard
the same idea again, said more simply
the decision both sides have accepted
a pause to lock something in before the next topic

see.where: You are in the Monday planning meeting. Your manager has just handed you a task and is already moving on to the next point.
see.asks: We need the new dashboard done soon — the usual metrics, same as last time. Can you take that?
see.goal: Don't just say yes. In about 30 seconds: say what is unclear, ask one precise question, say back what you heard, and confirm what you will do next.

hear.model: Sorry, one thing isn't clear to me yet. When you say soon, do you mean before Friday's review or by the end of the month? So you're saying the same six metrics as March, on the new dashboard. Then I'll build it with those six and have a first version to you by Thursday — does that work?
hear.note: Four moves, one each. The question names the exact gap — "soon". The last line is a plan and a request for a yes.

missions.prompt: We need the new dashboard done soon — the usual metrics, same as last time. Can you take that?
missions.context: "Soon" has not been defined: the quarterly review is on Friday and the board pack goes out at the end of the month. "The usual metrics" were the six numbers on the March dashboard — the sales team has since asked for two more. You could have a first version ready by Thursday.

see.where: A colleague from the client team calls you between meetings. She is in a hurry, and the line is not great.
see.who: A colleague from the client team, on the phone
see.asks: Can you sort out the client thing before the review? They're expecting it.
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Before you agree to anything, use the same four moves on an instruction you have not rehearsed.

missions.prompt: Can you sort out the client thing before the review? They're expecting it.
missions.context: There are two open items for this client: a revised quote, and the delivery date they asked about last week. The review is on Wednesday afternoon. You can send the quote today; the delivery date needs an answer from the warehouse, which usually replies within a day.

competencies.title: Explaining technical work to non-technical stakeholders
competencies.objective: Translate technical work into business language: say what it is in one plain sentence, explain what happens in everyday terms, say what it means for the person listening, and land the one thing they need to remember.
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The library has no product, business or tech explainer clip, and no title matches technical, simplify, jargon or non-technical. Caption text was scanned for this competency's own language. The closest is KDtidCsDGng ('Don't Scare, Inspire: How to Talk About AI Without Losing Your Audience', Think Fast Talk Smart, 26 min): a podcast conversation ABOUT making complex technology accessible — meet people where they are, give people examples, be clear on the takeaway — not a demonstration of explaining a piece of work to a stakeholder. It frames no work and states no impact, and its auto-captions carry 52 fillers, which is poor shadowing material. 1l1QFlbk8O8 ('A Simple Causal Phrase That Turns Any Data Point Into a Story') is about narrative causality when presenting data; 9G-QCNy57Hg and JZVh0-8QPgM are about speaking up in meetings and team design. Linking any of them would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow a product/business/tech explainer clip') has no clip in the library yet — a content gap to fill, at which point a reviewer can link it here.

moves.label: Frame it simply
moves.hint: Open with what the work is, or what it is for, in one plain sentence — and say out loud that you are keeping it simple. A listener who does not know what the thing is cannot follow how it works.
patterns: In simple terms, the checks are a set of tests that run before any report goes out.
Without getting too technical, the integration is a link between their shop and our warehouse.
The purpose of this process is to catch a broken number before anyone sees it.
moves.retry: Say it again and open with one plain sentence that says what the work is or what it is for — before you explain anything about how it works.
moves._cue_note: No bare "basically" or "essentially": the engine counts "basically" as a hedge, and a filler word cannot be the evidence that a learner framed the topic. Technical nouns are never cues — "the pipeline", "the API", "the schema" prove nothing about framing.

moves.label: Explain it plainly
moves.hint: Say what actually happens, in everyday words: a comparison, an example, or the steps in order. If you must use a technical word, say what it means straight after.
patterns: Behind the scenes, every night the system compares the new figures with last month's and flags anything that looks wrong.
Think of it like a spell-checker for numbers.
The way it works is that every order goes straight to the warehouse instead of being typed in each morning.
moves.retry: Say it again and explain what actually happens in everyday words — a comparison, an example, or the steps in order. No technical word without saying what it means.
cues: instead of doing it by hand
moves._cue_note: No bare "this means", "that means" or "which means": on its own each is neither a plain explanation nor an impact, and Week 2 already showed how easily it fires. An example or a comparison is credited because concreteness IS the behaviour; a technical verb on its own ("ingests", "validates") is not, and never appears here.

moves.label: Say what it means for them
moves.hint: The consequence for the person listening — their report, their customer, their time or their risk. Not what the system does; what changes for them.
patterns: What this means for you is that the month-end report can't go out with a broken number in it.
The benefit is that orders ship the same day and the typing mistakes stop.
The limitation is that returns aren't included yet.
moves.retry: Say it again and add what it means for the person listening — their report, their customer, their time or their risk. What changes for them, not what the system does.
cues: what this means is that you
what it means is that you
moves._cue_note: The consequence has to be named for the listener — "what this means for you", "the benefit is", "you no longer have to", "so that the team can". A bare "this means", a noun like "reporting", "the deadline" or "the cost", the word "impact" in a sentence about the system, or a prepositional phrase on its own ("for finance", "for the client") proves nothing and is not a cue — "we built it for finance" is not an impact statement. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Land the takeaway
moves.hint: Say the one thing they need to remember, then ask whether it landed. A stakeholder walks away with one sentence; make sure it is the right one.
patterns: The one thing to remember: if a report is late by a day, it's because a check caught something. Does that make sense?
The bottom line is that orders now ship the same day. Is that clear?
So the key point is that returns still need to be typed in. Does that answer it?
moves.retry: Say it again and finish with the one thing they need to remember — then ask whether it makes sense.
cues: the one thing to take away
does that sound right to you
moves._cue_note: Two things count: naming the takeaway ("the one thing to remember", "the bottom line") or asking whether it landed ("does that make sense?"). "The bottom line" sits here and not under impact, because the phrase bank teaches it as landing the key point, and a consequence stated without being singled out is impact, not a takeaway.

expressions.def: the words that open a simplified explanation
a way to signal that you are leaving the detail out on purpose
introduce a comparison with something the listener already knows
what the system does where nobody sees it
the words that turn a technical fact into a consequence for someone
state the value in one sentence
the single point that matters most, said last
ask whether the explanation landed

see.where: The finance director has stopped at your desk. She has heard the team spent two weeks on "data quality checks" and wants to know what that was for.
see.asks: So what exactly are these data quality checks you've all been working on? Keep it simple for me.
see.goal: In about 45 seconds, and without jargon: say what the checks are in plain terms, explain what happens, say what it means for her reports, and land the one thing she needs to remember.

hear.model: In simple terms, the checks are a set of tests that run before any report goes out. Behind the scenes, every night the system compares the new figures with last month's and flags anything that looks wrong — a region with no data, or a total ten times too big. What this means for you is that the month-end report can't go out with a broken number in it, so you stop finding mistakes in the board pack. The one thing to remember: if a report is a day late, it's because a check caught something. Does that make sense?
hear.note: Four moves in four breaths. Not one technical word — no schema, no pipeline, no job. The takeaway is one sentence, and it ends with a question.

missions.prompt: So what exactly are these data quality checks you've all been working on? Keep it simple for me.
missions.context: The checks are automated tests that run every night before the month-end report is built. They compare the new numbers with last month's and flag anything that looks wrong: a region with no data, a total ten times larger than usual. When a check fails, the report waits a day while someone looks. The finance director does not need to know how the checks are written; she needs to know what they do for her reports.

see.where: A colleague from sales catches you after the stand-up. Her client keeps asking about "the integration", and she has to answer by email this afternoon.
see.who: A colleague from sales, who will repeat your words to the client
see.asks: Can you explain what the integration actually does? I need to put it in plain words for the client.
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time, and your words will be passed on to someone you will never meet. Use the same four moves on work you have not rehearsed explaining.

missions.prompt: Can you explain what the integration actually does? I need to put it in plain words for the client.
missions.context: The integration connects the client's online shop to your warehouse system. Each time a customer orders, the order goes to the warehouse automatically instead of being typed in by hand every morning. It went live last week. It does not yet handle returns — those are still entered by hand. For the client it means orders ship the same day and the typing mistakes stop.

competencies.title: Recommendations & decision language
competencies.objective: Stop only reporting; start recommending: lay out the options on the table, recommend one, give the reason, name the trade-off honestly, and propose the next step so a decision can be made.
competencies.pattern: OPTIONS → RECOMMENDATION → REASON → TRADE-OFF → NEXT STEP
competencies._shadow_note: No shadow block, after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (2026-09-23). The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow a clip of a manager or consultant giving recommendations') has no clip in the library: no title matches recommend, decision, option or trade-off in a workplace sense, and a caption scan for this competency's own language found no clip that recommends one option, gives the reason, names the trade-off and proposes the next step. The closest is 2gIaaPT_-Ag ('Stop Overthinking: How to Fix Your Decision Making Skills', Indeed, 8 min, human captions): a lesson on deciding for yourself — list your options, weight the criteria, score them, 'the next step is to choose' — not on communicating a recommendation to someone else; it never recommends, reasons aloud or names a trade-off. pGSxI_2RnTY ('7 Key Tensions Every Leader Must Balance') mentions the downsides of leadership styles; 0zzQ1jth6Cw ('How AI Is Ruining Job Interviews') and 9vG1ib2gF-k ('The Persuasion Equation') contain 'I recommend' and 'trade-off' in passing. Linking any of them would produce supporting evidence that is not about this competency. Content-library gap: a manager or consultant giving a recommendation; a reviewer can link it here when one is added.

moves.label: Lay out the options
moves.hint: Name the choices on the table — two or three, one short line each — before you say which one. A listener who has not heard the options cannot weigh your recommendation.
patterns: We have two options here.
Option A is to wait for the original supplier; option B is to order from the second supplier.
There are two ways we could go: send it tomorrow, or hold it for two days.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by naming the options — two or three, one line each — before you say which one you recommend.
moves._cue_note: Naming an option by letter is not this move: "I'd recommend option B" has not laid anything out, so a bare "option A" or "option B" is never a cue — only "option A is…", "we have two options", "one option is… the other…". "We could…", "maybe…" and "or we could…" belong here too: they present a possibility, they do not choose one, and they never prove a recommendation.

moves.label: Recommend one
moves.hint: Say which option you recommend, in one clear sentence. Not a preference, not a maybe — the one you would put your name to.
patterns: I'd recommend option B.
My recommendation is to hold the report.
The lowest-risk option would be to order from the second supplier.
moves.retry: Say it again and commit to ONE option in one plain sentence — "I'd recommend…" or "My recommendation is…" — not "I think" and not "maybe".
moves._cue_note: No "I think", "I suggest", "maybe", "we could", "better" or "good": "I think A is better" is a preference, not a recommendation, and "I suggest" is how people hedge one. Only a first-person commitment to one option counts — "I'd recommend", "my recommendation is", "I'd go with". "The best option is…" counts because it names a judgement, not a feeling. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Give the reason
moves.hint: Why that option — the fact that decides it. One reason said clearly beats three said vaguely.
patterns: The main reason is that the customer has already been told the 15th.
It's based on the quality check they passed last time.
From a delivery perspective, it's the only option that keeps the date.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the reason for your recommendation — the fact that decides it — "the main reason is…" or "based on…", not just "because".
cues: it is the only option that
moves._cue_note: No bare "because" and no bare "since": "because the bus was late" is not a justification for a decision, and a learner who says "because" has not necessarily given a reason that decides anything. What counts is a stated justification — "the main reason is", "based on", "given that", a comparative merit ("it's cheaper", "lower risk") or a perspective ("from a delivery perspective"). A reason with no recommendation is still not a recommendation; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Name the trade-off
moves.hint: What the recommended option costs, or when the other one would win. Saying it first is what makes a recommendation trustworthy.
patterns: The trade-off is the 20% — about two thousand pounds on this order.
The downside is that it's the first late report we've ever sent them.
If speed is the priority, then option B; if cost is, option A.
moves.retry: Say it again and name the trade-off honestly — what the option you recommend costs, or when the other one would be the right choice.
cues: if risk reduction is the priority
would be the right call if
moves._cue_note: No bare "but", "although" or "however": "although I was late" is not a trade-off. What counts is a named cost ("the trade-off is", "the downside", "it costs more") or a condition under which the other option wins ("if speed is the priority, then…"). A trade-off stated with no recommendation behind it is honesty about nothing; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Propose the next step
moves.hint: What happens if they agree — who does what, and how you get the decision. Close so the listener can say yes.
patterns: If you agree, the next step is that I'll place the order this afternoon.
So the next step is that you tell the client today, and I'll rerun it as soon as the source is fixed.
Here's what I suggest we do next: I confirm with them tomorrow and you sign off by Wednesday.
moves.retry: Say it again and close with the next step — who does what if they agree — and ask for the decision.
cues: what i suggest we do next
what i'd suggest we do next
what i'd like to do next
what i would like to do next
if you are happy with that
if you give me the go-ahead
do you want me to go ahead
would you like me to go ahead
moves._cue_note: A deadline is not a next step: "by Friday" on its own proves nothing, and no day or date is a cue. What counts is the action that follows agreement — who does what ("I'll place the order", "you tell the client") — or the request for the decision itself ("if you agree", "I need a decision by", "shall I go ahead?").

expressions.def: the sentence that puts the choices on the table before you weigh them
commit to one option in your own name
the choice that can go wrong least — name it when that is what you are recommending
point to the fact or evidence that decides it
name the angle your reason comes from — delivery, cost, risk, quality
what the option you recommend costs, said before anyone asks
the condition under which one option beats the other

expressions.w: here's what I suggest we do next
expressions.def: close with the action, so a decision can be made

see.where: Your project lead has ten minutes before the steering meeting. The supplier's part is going to be late, and she needs a recommendation, not a status.
see.asks: The supplier's part is going to be three weeks late. What do you recommend we do?
see.goal: Don't just describe the options. In about 45 seconds: lay them out, recommend one, give the reason, name the trade-off, and propose the next step so she can decide.

hear.model: We have two options here. Option A is to wait for the original supplier: no extra cost, but the part comes in three weeks and the go-live slips to the end of the month. Option B is to order from the second supplier: one week, twenty percent more, and the go-live date holds. What I'd recommend is option B. The main reason is that the customer has already been told the fifteenth, and keeping that date is worth more than the extra cost. The trade-off is the twenty percent — about two thousand pounds on this order. If you agree, the next step is that I'll place the order this afternoon and confirm the delivery date with them by tomorrow.
hear.note: Five moves, in order, and a real choice at the centre. The reason is one fact, the trade-off is a number, and the last line hands her the decision.

missions.prompt: The supplier's part is going to be three weeks late. What do you recommend we do?
missions.context: Two options. Option A: wait for the original supplier — the part arrives in three weeks, no extra cost, but the customer's go-live slips from the 15th to the end of the month. Option B: order the part from a second supplier who can deliver in one week at 20% more — about £2,000 on this order — and the go-live date holds; that supplier passed the quality check last time. The customer has already been told the 15th.

see.where: The customer success manager stops you in the corridor. A client's monthly report has wrong numbers in it because of a data issue, and it is due to the client tomorrow morning.
see.who: The customer success manager, who will decide what to tell the client
see.asks: We've found the numbers are wrong. What do you recommend — do we send it or hold it?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Lay out the two choices you were given, recommend one, give the reason, name the trade-off, and propose the next step.

missions.prompt: We've found the numbers are wrong. What do you recommend — do we send it or hold it?
missions.context: Two choices. Send the report tomorrow as planned with the wrong numbers corrected by hand — that takes tonight, and two of the twelve charts cannot be checked in time. Or hold the report for two days, fix the data source and rerun everything — the client gets it late, but every chart is checked. The client has never had a late report from you; last quarter they complained about a wrong figure.

competencies.title: Disagreeing professionally & pushing back
competencies.objective: Stop swallowing your disagreement, and stop blurting it: acknowledge what is right about their proposal, say plainly where you differ, give the reason, offer a way forward, and close on the goal you share — so you sound neither aggressive nor weak.

shadow.title: 925 English Lesson 11 - How to Disagree and Say No in English
shadow.why: A lesson on this exact job, with repeat-after-me practice: disagreeing carefully ('I'm not sure that's the best option here', 'I'm afraid I don't totally agree'), then the 'yes, but' shape — say what is good about the idea, then the difference and the reason ('Good idea, but we don't have enough time'; 'I know experience is important, but she's not a good fit') — and a short co-worker dialogue about whether to hire someone. It models three of the five moves — acknowledge, disagree and reason — and not the alternative or the close, so it supports this competency without standing in for it. Its last section, disagreeing strongly ('That's out of the question', 'You've got to be kidding'), is the tone this week teaches you to avoid: shadow the careful and 'yes, but' sections, not that one.

competencies._shadow_note: Linked after a content check of the 301-clip catalogue (315 caption files, 2026-09-23). A title and caption scan for disagree, push back, concern, objection, politely, respectfully and the competency's own phrases found 29 clips with 'disagree' in the captions; the strongest were read in context. Linked: mmfo9spNaWA (Business English Pod, 10 min, human captions, in the Meetings shelf) — see shadow.why for what it models and what it does not. Runners-up, and why each is insufficient: jCYLhRKMk8A ('Responding to Suggestions in English', Business English Pod) is a close second — a meeting where suggestions are turned down with 'that's a good idea, but I'm not sure it would work — for one thing…' — but it is framed as rejecting a suggestion, offers no alternative or close, and its captions are rougher; nT5dB9SDJPA ('Why You're Bad at Disagreeing', HBR IdeaCast, 31 min) is an interview ABOUT being open to disagreement, not a model of doing it; whKyHP5vc3I ('5 Phrases for Difficult Conversations') has one pushback example ('I wish it were possible to deliver by Friday, but quality requires proper testing time') among five general softeners; WH4ge8WjhZM (assertive communication) is about stating your own needs, not answering a proposal; _qbT2sNlPGo (saying no politely) declines requests rather than pushing back on a plan; 4mg_x8yndyQ (expressing doubt) stops at doubt. The curriculum's Monday task ('Shadow a clip of polite disagreement / discussion') is met by the linked clip for the first three moves. No clip in the library shows a professional proposing an alternative and closing on the shared goal — that half of the Monday task is a content-library gap, and a reviewer can relink here when a full pushback clip is added.

moves.label: Acknowledge their point
moves.hint: Show you heard the proposal and what is right about it — one line — before you say where you differ. A listener who feels heard can hear a no.
patterns: I see the reasoning — the demo is Monday and a live portal makes a stronger pitch.
That's a fair point; speed matters on this one.
I understand why you want it out this week.
moves.retry: Say it again and open by showing you heard them — "I see the reasoning…", "That's a fair point…", "I understand why…" — before you say where you differ.
cues: i see where you're coming from
i see where you are coming from
i understand where you're coming from
i understand where you are coming from
i know where you're coming from
i hear what you are saying
i'm on board with the goal
there is a lot to like
i would love to say yes
moves._cue_note: A bare "yes", "okay", "sure" or "right" is not acknowledgement, and neither is "with respect" or "actually". What counts is naming what is right about their position — "I see the reasoning", "that's a fair point", "I understand why you want…". "I see your point" credits THIS move and nothing else: it proves the learner heard, not that they differ. A learner who acknowledges and then agrees has made one move of five.

moves.label: Say where you differ
moves.hint: State your position plainly — one concern, named. Not "I'm not sure", not "maybe": a difference they can actually hear.
patterns: I have one concern: I don't think we should launch the full portal on Friday.
I'd push back on the timeline.
My hesitation is the payment flow — I'm not convinced it's ready.
moves.retry: Say it again and state your actual position — "I have one concern…", "I don't think we should…", "I'd push back on…" — not "I'm not sure" and not "maybe".
cues: i am going to push back
i don't think we are ready
i don't think that will work
i don't think this will work
i don't think it will work
i don't think that's the right
i don't think that is the right
i don't think that's the best
i don't think that is the best
i don't think this is the right
i don't think this is the best
i'm not sure that will work
i'm not sure that would work
i'm not sure that's the right
i'm not sure that is the right
i'm not sure that's the best
i'm not sure that's the way
i'm not sure we are ready
i'm not sure it will work
i'm not sure it's the right
i am not in favour of
i am not in favor of
that is not going to work
we can't do all of it
moves._cue_note: The move most exposed to false positives, so the bar is a stated difference of position: "I have one concern", "I don't think we should…", "I'd push back on…", "I'm not convinced it's ready". Never "I think…", "maybe…", "however…", "but…", "with respect" or "actually" — those are frames with nothing inside them — and never "I'm not sure" on its own: only "I'm not sure that will work" / "we should" / "we're ready", where an object follows. "I see your point" is acknowledgement; "I suggest", "I recommend", "another option" and "we could" are at most a way forward — none of them proves a difference of position. "Can I offer a different perspective?" asks permission and proves nothing until the perspective follows. Under-crediting is the safe direction: the AI pass may ADD a move it heard in the learner's own words and can never remove one.

moves.label: Give the reason
moves.hint: The fact or risk behind your concern — data, delivery, quality. One concrete reason beats a vague worry.
patterns: The risk of moving too quickly is the payment flow: two of the five tests are still failing.
The reason is that last release, a launch without a full test run cost us a week of fixes.
Based on the pilot, the switch took two weeks to settle.
moves.retry: Say it again and give the reason — the fact or risk behind your concern — "the risk is…", "the reason is…", "based on…", not just "because".
cues: if we go live on friday
if we do it in one go
if we do everything at once
from a delivery point of view
from a quality point of view
from a risk point of view
moves._cue_note: No bare "because" and no bare "since": "because I said so" is not a reason. What counts is a named risk or fact — "the risk of moving too quickly is", "the reason is", "based on the pilot", "two of the five tests are still failing", "last release cost us a week". A reason with no stated position is a worry, not a pushback; the bar is every move.

moves.label: Offer a way forward
moves.hint: Don't stop at no. Say what you would do instead — a check first, a smaller step, a later date — so the pushback has somewhere to go.
patterns: What I'd suggest is that we go live on Friday with everything except payments, and switch payments on once the tests pass.
Could we validate the payment flow first and announce the date on Monday?
What if we switched the night team first, since they're already trained, and brought the day shifts across two weeks later?
moves.retry: Say it again and offer a way forward — "What I'd suggest is…", "What if we…", "Could we… instead" — so your no has somewhere to go.
moves._cue_note: A way forward, not a wish: "I'd suggest we validate first", "what if we…", "could we push it to Tuesday". "Another option" on its own lists, it does not propose, and "we could" on its own is a possibility — neither is a cue. "I suggest" and "I recommend" credit this move only when an action follows ("I'd suggest we…"), and never prove disagreement: a suggestion with no stated difference is agreement with extra steps. An alternative with no position behind it is one move of five.

moves.label: Close on the shared goal
moves.hint: End on what you both want and hand the decision back — so it lands as help, not a fight.
patterns: That way we still have a live portal for Monday — does that work for you?
We both want this out the door before December.
If you'd still rather go Friday, I'll flag the risk in writing — but I'd ask for the two extra days.
moves.retry: Say it again and close on the shared goal — "that way we still…", "we both want…", "does that work for you?" — and hand the decision back.
cues: i want to make this work
a way that works for both
moves._cue_note: The move that keeps a pushback from being a fight: the shared goal named ("we both want this out before December", "that way we still have it live for Monday") or the decision handed back ("does that work for you?", "if you'd still rather go Friday, I'll flag the risk"). A deadline or a date proves nothing here, and "the same thing" or "let's get it done" on their own do not name a shared goal. "Does that work?" is also Week 4's confirm — each competency grades on its own moves, so that is fine.

expressions.def: show you heard the case for their proposal before you answer it
name what is right about their position — the line that makes a no hearable
state a difference of position without a fight — one concern, named
voice the concern softly, but as a position — not a maybe
signal disagreement a room can hear — soft in tone, clear in position

expressions.w: the risk of moving too quickly is
expressions.def: frame the reason as a risk — the fact behind the concern
propose a check first — the way forward that turns a no into a plan
close on the shared goal — what your alternative keeps for both of you

see.where: Wednesday stand-up. Your product manager wants to bring the launch of the new customer portal forward from next Wednesday to this Friday, because sales have a big demo on Monday. You run the testing, and the payment tests are not finished.
see.who: Your product manager, in front of the team
see.asks: Let's launch the portal this Friday instead of next Wednesday. The demo is Monday and I want it live. Any reason we can't?
see.goal: Push back without sounding aggressive or weak. In about 45 seconds: acknowledge why she wants Friday, say plainly where you differ, give the reason, offer a way forward, and close on the goal you share.

hear.model: I see the reasoning — the demo is Monday, and a live portal makes a stronger pitch. I have one concern, though: I don't think we should launch the full portal on Friday. The risk of moving too quickly is the payment flow. Two of the five payment tests are still failing, and last release a launch without a full test run cost us a week of fixes. What I'd suggest is that we go live on Friday with everything except payments, which is what the demo needs anyway, and switch payments on next Wednesday once the tests pass. That way we still have a live portal for Monday, and nobody sees a broken checkout. Does that work for you?
hear.note: Five moves, in order, and no apology. The acknowledgement names what is right about Friday, the concern is a position, the reason is a fact, the alternative gives her most of what she wants, and the last line hands the decision back.

missions.prompt: Let's launch the portal this Friday instead of next Wednesday. The demo is Monday and I want it live. Any reason we can't?
missions.context: The plan was to launch next Wednesday. Sales have a demo on Monday to two prospects; it uses a demo account and does not need the payment flow. As of today, two of the five payment tests are still failing, and the payment tests are due to finish on Tuesday next week. Last release, a launch without a full test run cost the team a week of fixes and three customer complaints. Everything except payments is ready now.

see.where: Your team lead has just come out of planning. The operations director wants the whole warehouse moved to the new stock system in one go, over the last weekend of November. You ran the pilot at the small depot.
see.who: Your team lead, who has to reply to the director this afternoon
see.asks: The director wants the whole warehouse on the new stock system in one go, over the last weekend of November. She thinks a phased move just drags it out. You ran the pilot — what do you think?
see.goal: Nobody is prompting you this time. Acknowledge the director's reasoning, say plainly where you differ, give the reason, offer a way forward, and close on the goal you share.

missions.prompt: The director wants the whole warehouse on the new stock system in one go, over the last weekend of November. She thinks a phased move just drags it out. You ran the pilot — what do you think?
missions.context: At the pilot depot, the switch took two weeks to settle: 40 stock counts were wrong in the first week. The main warehouse holds 20 times the stock of the pilot depot. December is the busiest month, and the two systems cannot run side by side, so a failed weekend switch means counting by hand until it is fixed. The director's reason for one go is that a phased move drags it out. The night team has already been trained on the new system; the day shifts have not.
